context: D. Profits ineligible for payment of dividend. 10. (2) If the audit report by the statutory auditor contains a modified opinion that indicates an overstatement of the PAT, the same shall not be available for payment of dividend, to the extent it is included in PAT.
question: What categories of profit are excluded from dividend payment eligibility under the RBI SFB Dividend Directions, 2026?
YOUR_ANSWER: Two categories of profit are excluded. First, any exceptional and/or extra-ordinary profits or income cannot be used for dividend payment. Second, if the statutory auditor's report contains a modified opinion indicating an overstatement of Profit After Tax (PAT), that overstated portion is also excluded from dividend eligibility.

context: Regulation 8(10): Where the acquirer or persons acting in concert acquires shares of the target company during the period of twenty-six weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price under these regulations, the acquirer and persons acting in concert shall pay the difference between the highest acquisition price and the offer price, to all the shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer, within sixty days from the date of such acquisition.
question: Under Regulation 8(10), if an acquirer buys shares of the target company within 26 weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price, what obligation arises and within what timeframe must it be fulfilled?
YOUR_ANSWER: If the acquirer or persons acting in concert purchase shares of the target company within 26 weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the open offer price, they are obligated to pay the difference between that higher acquisition price and the original offer price to all shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer. This payment must be made within 60 days from the date of such acquisition.

question: Under SEBI NCS Regulations 2021, what is the minimum notice period that an issuer must provide to holders of non-convertible securities before a buy-back right becomes exercisable?
YOUR_ANSWER: The issuer must provide at least 21 days' notice to all eligible holders of non-convertible securities and the debenture trustee before the date from which the buy-back right becomes exercisable.

context: Regulation 10(f) (as amended by SEBI (AIF) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2025, w.e.f. 19-11-2025): no scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have more than one thousand investors: Provided that accredited investors shall be excluded while computing the number of investors in a scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund. question: What change did the SEBI (AIF) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2025 make to how the 1,000-investor cap is calculated for an AIF scheme?
YOUR_ANSWER: Before the amendment, all investors — including accredited investors — were counted toward the 1,000-investor cap for an AIF scheme. The SEBI (AIF) (Third Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective 19 November 2025, changed this so that accredited investors are now excluded when computing the number of investors, effectively allowing more flexibility in scheme composition.

context:
Passage A:
Regulation 16(1)(c) (pre-2024): Category I Alternative Investment Funds shall not borrow funds directly or indirectly or engage in any leverage except for meeting temporary funding requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year and not more than ten percent of the investable funds.

Passage B:
Regulation 16(1)(c) (as substituted w.e.f. 07-08-2024): Category I Alternative Investment Funds shall not borrow funds directly or indirectly or engage in any leverage for the purpose of making investments or otherwise, except for borrowing funds to meet temporary funding requirements and day-to-day operational requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year and not more than ten percent of the investable funds.
question: Do the pre-2024 and post-2024 versions of Regulation 16(1)(c) permit the same scope of borrowing by Category I AIFs?
YOUR_ANSWER: Not entirely. Both versions agree on the basic parameters — borrowing limited to 30 days, not more than 4 occasions a year, and not exceeding 10% of investable funds. However, the post-2024 version is slightly broader in scope: it explicitly covers borrowing for both 'day-to-day operational requirements' in addition to 'temporary funding requirements,' which was not mentioned in the pre-2024 version. So the permitted purpose of borrowing was expanded, even though the quantitative limits remain the same.

context: "independent research analyst" means a person whose only business activity is research analysis or preparation and/or publication of research report.
question: Under SEBI (Research Analysts) Regulations 2014, who qualifies as an 'independent research analyst'?
YOUR_ANSWER: An 'independent research analyst' is a person whose sole business activity is research analysis or the preparation and/or publication of research reports. They must not be engaged in any other business activity.

context: Regulation 10(d): the Manager or Sponsor shall have a continuing interest in the Alternative Investment Fund of not less than two and half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower, in the form of investment in the Alternative Investment Fund.
question: A Category I AIF has a total corpus of Rs 300 crore. What is the minimum continuing interest the Manager or Sponsor must maintain in this fund under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: The continuing interest must be the lower of 2.5% of the corpus or Rs 5 crore. For a corpus of Rs 300 crore, 2.5% works out to Rs 7.5 crore. Since Rs 5 crore is lower than Rs 7.5 crore, the minimum continuing interest the Manager or Sponsor must maintain is Rs 5 crore.

question: A mutual fund scheme with net assets of Rs500 crore needs to borrow for redemption pressure. What is the maximum it may borrow, and for what maximum duration?
YOUR_ANSWER: The mutual fund may borrow a maximum of 20% of the net assets of the scheme, which comes to Rs 100 crore (20% of Rs 500 crore). The borrowing duration cannot exceed 6 months.

context: The promoters shall hold at least twenty per cent. of the post-issue capital: Provided that in case the post-issue shareholding of the promoters is less than twenty per cent., alternative investment funds, or foreign venture capital investors, or scheduled commercial banks, or public financial institutions, or insurance companies registered with the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India or any non-individual public shareholder holding at least five per cent. of the post-issue capital may contribute to meet the shortfall in minimum contribution as specified for the promoters, subject to a maximum of ten per cent. of the post-issue capital.
question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, what is the minimum percentage of post-issue capital that promoters must hold following a public issue?
YOUR_ANSWER: Promoters must hold at least 20% of the post-issue capital. If their shareholding falls below this, certain specified entities — such as AIFs, foreign venture capital investors, scheduled commercial banks, public financial institutions, IRDAI-registered insurance companies, or any non-individual public shareholder holding at least 5% of the post-issue capital — may contribute to meet the shortfall, but each such entity's contribution is capped at 10% of the post-issue capital.

context: Eligibility criteria. 7. question: Under the 2023 amendment to Regulation 7, if a sponsor fails all eligibility requirements, what are the three key obligations: the AMC capitalization threshold, the lock-in period, and the minimum combined experience of the five senior officers?
YOUR_ANSWER: If a sponsor fails to meet the eligibility requirements, three obligations apply: (1) The AMC must be adequately capitalized with a net worth of not less than Rs 150 crore; (2) The initial shareholding equivalent to the Rs 150 crore capital contribution must be locked in for a period of 5 years; and (3) The combined experience of the CEO, COO, CRO, CCO, and CIO must total at least 30 years.

context: Regulation 21(1): The Investment Adviser shall redress investor grievances promptly but not later than twenty-one calendar days from the date of receipt of the grievance and in such manner as may be specified by the Board.
question: What is the maximum time limit within which an investment adviser must redress investor grievances under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013?
YOUR_ANSWER: An investment adviser must redress investor grievances within a maximum of 21 calendar days from the date the grievance is received.

question: What is the total amount of Government of India dated securities to be issued during the first half of FY 2026-27, i.e., April to September 2026?
YOUR_ANSWER: The total amount of Government of India dated securities to be issued during the first half of FY 2026-27 (April to September 2026) is Rs 8,20,000 crore.

context: Regulation 15(1)(e): Alternative Investment Fund shall not invest except with the approval of seventy five percent of investors by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund in — (a) associates; or (b) units of Alternative Investment Funds managed or sponsored by its Manager, Sponsor or associates of its Manager or Sponsor.
question: Under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012, what investor approval is required before an AIF can invest in its associate companies or in units of other AIFs managed by the same manager or sponsor?
YOUR_ANSWER: Before an AIF can invest in its associate companies or in units of other AIFs managed or sponsored by the same manager, sponsor, or their associates, approval from at least 75% of investors by value of their investment in the AIF is required.

context: Regulation 19(3): An investment adviser shall conduct yearly audit in respect of compliance with these regulations from a member of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India or Institute of Company Secretaries of India or Institute of Cost Accountants of India and submit a report of the same as may be specified by the Board.
question: What type of audit is required of an investment adviser under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013, and who is qualified to conduct it?
YOUR_ANSWER: An investment adviser is required to conduct a yearly compliance audit under SEBI IA Regulations, 2013. This audit must be conducted by a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), or the Institute of Cost Accountants of India (ICoAI). The audit report must be submitted as specified by SEBI.

context: Regulation 14(g) (original): the client shall agree to obtain a rating from at least two different rating agencies for any issue of debt securities whose size is equal to or exceeds, rupees one hundred crores. [Substituted by SEBI (CRA) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2011, w.e.f. 27-12-2011]: the client shall obtain a rating for any issue of debt securities in accordance with the relevant regulations.
question: Under the original SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, what was the mandatory dual-rating requirement for large debt issues, and when was it removed?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under the original SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, any debt issue of Rs 100 crore or more was required to obtain ratings from at least two different rating agencies — a mandatory dual-rating requirement. This requirement was removed and substituted by the SEBI (CRA) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2011, effective 27 December 2011, which simply required the client to obtain a rating in accordance with the relevant regulations, without specifying a minimum of two agencies.

context: Regulation 7(1): The open offer for acquiring shares to be made under regulation 3 and regulation 4 shall be for at least twenty six per cent of total shares of the target company, as of tenth working day from the closure of the tendering period.
question: A listed company has 50 crore shares outstanding. An acquirer acquires shares triggering a mandatory open offer under Regulation 3(1). What is the minimum number of shares for which the open offer must be made under Regulation 7(1)?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 7(1), the open offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares of the target company. With 50 crore shares outstanding, the minimum number of shares for which the open offer must be made is 26% of 50 crore, which equals 13 crore shares.

question: Do Section A and Section B of the RBI Master Direction on Unique Identifiers in Financial Markets 2026 both come into force on the same date?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they do not come into force on the same date. Section A on the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) comes into force with immediate effect upon issuance, while Section B on the Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) comes into effect only from January 01, 2027.

question: Do Passage A and Passage B permit the same range of additional business activities for an AMC?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the two passages do not permit the same range of activities. Passage A (the older version) allows a broader set of additional activities, including portfolio management services, financial consultancy, exchange of research on commercial basis, and management of venture capital funds. Passage B (the revised version) narrows the permitted activities to management and advisory services for pooled assets such as offshore funds, insurance funds, pension funds, provident funds, and certain categories of foreign portfolio investors. YOUR_ANSWER: The maximum permissible interval between two consecutive unit holders' meetings is 15 months.

question: Which was enacted earlier — the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations 2009 or the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations 2018?
YOUR_ANSWER: The SEBI (ICDR) Regulations 2009 were enacted earlier. The 2018 regulations superseded the 2009 regulations.

context: Regulation 28A(1): The Board may, exempt any person or class of persons from the operation of all or any of the provisions of these regulations for a period as may be specified but not exceeding twelve months, for furthering innovation relating to testing new products, processes, services, business models, etc. in live environment of regulatory sandbox in the securities markets.
question: A fintech company seeks a regulatory sandbox exemption from SEBI under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013. SEBI grants an initial exemption of 8 months. If SEBI grants an extension, what is the maximum total duration of the regulatory sandbox exemption permissible under these regulations?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 28A(1), the maximum total duration of a regulatory sandbox exemption is 12 months. Since SEBI has already granted an initial exemption of 8 months, any extension cannot push the total beyond 12 months. Therefore, the maximum permissible extension would be 4 months, and the total sandbox period cannot exceed 12 months in any case.

context:

Passage B:
Regulation 13(5) (as amended): Extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund: Provided that an Accredited Investors only fund may be permitted to extend its tenure up to five years subject to the approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Accredited Investors only fund.
question: Do these two versions of Regulation 13(5) prescribe the same maximum tenure extension period for all close-ended AIFs?
YOUR_ANSWER: Not for all AIFs. For regular close-ended AIFs, both versions agree that the maximum tenure extension is 2 years, subject to approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value. However, the amended version (Passage B) introduces an additional provision: Accredited Investors only funds may extend their tenure by up to 5 years, again subject to the same two-thirds approval threshold. So the two versions are not identical — the amended version allows a longer maximum extension for a specific category of fund.

question: Under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, what is the maximum percentage of total mutual fund transactions that may be routed through a broker associated with the sponsor, and over what period is this limit measured?
YOUR_ANSWER: An AMC cannot route more than 5% of the aggregate purchases and sales of securities by the mutual fund across all its schemes through a broker associated with the sponsor. This limit is measured over a block of any three months.

question: Do Bucket B1 and Bucket B10 permit the same dividend payout as a percentage of Adjusted PAT under the RBI SFB Dividend Directions 2026?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they do not. Bucket B10, applicable where the Tier 1 Capital Ratio is above 19.5%, allows up to 100% of Adjusted PAT to be paid as dividend. The permitted payout is entirely different.

question: What change did the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 make to the definition of 'credit rating agency' under Regulation 2(h)?
YOUR_ANSWER: Before the amendment, the definition of 'credit rating agency' under Regulation 2(h) was limited to rating of securities offered by way of public or rights issue. The SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021, effective 3 August 2021, expanded this to cover rating of securities that are listed or proposed to be listed on a stock exchange recognized by SEBI. YOUR_ANSWER: The sponsor must have an average net annual profit (after depreciation, interest, and tax) of at least Rs 10 crore over the immediately preceding five years to meet the 'sound track record' requirement.

question: For how long is an applicant barred from making a fresh registration application if their application is rejected for containing false or misleading information?
YOUR_ANSWER: An applicant whose application is rejected for containing false or misleading information is barred from making any fresh application for registration — whether under these regulations or any other SEBI regulations — for a period of one year from the date of such rejection.

YOUR_ANSWER: The grievance was lodged on March 5, 2025. Adding 21 calendar days, the regulatory deadline for the investment adviser to redress it is March 26, 2025.

context: Regulation 4: The Board shall not consider an application under regulation 3 unless the applicant is promoted by a person belonging to any of the following categories: (a) a public financial institution; (b) a scheduled commercial bank included in the second schedule to the RBI Act, 1934; (c) a foreign bank operating in India with the approval of the Reserve Bank of India; (d) a foreign credit rating agency incorporated in a Financial Action Task Force (FATF) member jurisdiction and recognised under their law, having a minimum of five years' experience in rating securities; (e) any company or body corporate having continuous net worth of minimum rupees one hundred crores as per audited annual accounts for the previous five years.
question: Who are the eligible categories of promoters for a credit rating agency under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 4 of SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, the eligible categories of promoters for a credit rating agency are: (a) a public financial institution; (b) a scheduled commercial bank listed in the second schedule to the RBI Act, 1934; (c) a foreign bank operating in India with RBI approval; (d) a foreign credit rating agency incorporated in a FATF member jurisdiction and recognized under their law, with at least five years' experience in rating securities; and (e) a company or body corporate with continuous net worth of at least Rs 100 crore as per audited annual accounts for the previous five years.

question: What ongoing net worth requirement must a credit rating agency maintain at all times under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? What transitional relief was provided for existing CRAs?
YOUR_ANSWER: A credit rating agency must maintain a minimum net worth of Rs 25 crore at all times. As a transitional measure, CRAs that were already registered with SEBI and had a net worth below Rs 25 crore were given a period of three years from the date of notification of the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 to increase their net worth to this level.

context: Regulation 7(1): An individual investment adviser or a principal officer of a non-individual investment adviser registered as an investment adviser under these regulations or persons associated with investment advice, shall have the following minimum qualification, at all times — (a) A graduate degree or any equivalent educational qualification from a university or institution recognized by the Central Government or any State Government or a recognised foreign university or institution or association or CFA Charter from the CFA Institute, and relevant certification from NISM or from any other organization or institution accredited by NISM; or (c) A Post Graduate Program in the Securities Market (Investment Advisory) from NISM or a Post Graduate Program in Financial Planning from NISM or any other program of NISM as may be specified by the Board.
question: What are the minimum qualification requirements for an individual investment adviser under the SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 (as currently amended)?
YOUR_ANSWER: An individual investment adviser (or the principal officer of a non-individual IA, or persons associated with investment advice) must meet one of the following: (a) A graduate degree from a recognized university or institution (Indian or foreign), or a CFA Charter from the CFA Institute, along with relevant NISM certification or certification from an NISM-accredited body; or (c) A Post Graduate Program in Securities Market (Investment Advisory) or Financial Planning from NISM, or any other NISM program as specified by SEBI.

question: How many years elapsed between the issuance of the first LEI circular (June 01, 2017) and its supersession by the Master Direction on Unique Identifiers (March 27, 2026)?
YOUR_ANSWER: The first LEI circular was issued on June 01, 2017, and it was superseded by the Master Direction on March 27, 2026. That is approximately 8 years and 9 months — or just under 9 years — between the two dates.

question: What restrictions apply to the activities a credit rating agency may undertake under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: A credit rating agency is restricted to rating securities that are listed or proposed to be listed on a SEBI-recognized stock exchange. It cannot engage in any other business activity. YOUR_ANSWER: If the market participant is unable to obtain the UTI within the required reporting deadline for a cross-border transaction, they are allowed up to five Mumbai business days from the date of the transaction to obtain and submit the UTI to CCIL-TR.

question: Under SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008, within how many days must SEBI dispose of a complete prior approval request for change in status or constitution? What is deemed to happen if SEBI fails to communicate its decision within this period?

question: All schemes of a mutual fund together hold 9.5% of ABC Limited's paid-up capital carrying voting rights. May they acquire a further 1%?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they may not acquire the additional 1%. The regulation states that no mutual fund under all its schemes should own more than 10% of any company's paid-up capital carrying voting rights. Currently holding 9.5%, acquiring a further 1% would take the total to 10.5%, which exceeds the 10% cap. Therefore, the acquisition is not permitted.

context:
Passage A:
A mutual fund scheme shall not invest more than 5% of its NAV in the unlisted equity shares or equity related instruments in case of open ended scheme and 10% of its NAV in case of close ended scheme.

Passage B:
All investments by a mutual fund scheme in equity shares and equity related instruments shall only be made provided such securities are listed or to be listed.
question: Do Passage A and Passage B permit mutual fund schemes to hold any unlisted equity instruments?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they do not agree. Passage A permits mutual fund schemes to hold unlisted equity shares or equity-related instruments up to 5% of NAV for open-ended schemes and up to 10% for close-ended schemes. Passage B, on the other hand, completely prohibits any investment in unlisted equity by requiring all such investments to be in listed or to-be-listed securities. The two passages are directly contradictory on this point.

context: Asset management company and its obligations. 25. (26) The asset management company shall ensure that no change in the fundamental attributes of any scheme or the trust, fees and expenses payable or any other change which would modify the scheme and affect the interest of unit holders, shall be carried out unless,— (i) a written communication about the proposed change is sent to each unit holder and an advertisement is issued in one English daily newspaper having nationwide circulation as well as in a newspaper published in the language of region where the Head Office of the mutual fund is situated; and (ii) the unit holders are given an option to exit at the prevailing Net Asset Value without any exit load.
question: What two conditions must an AMC satisfy before making any change to the fundamental attributes of a mutual fund scheme?
YOUR_ANSWER: Before changing any fundamental attributes of a mutual fund scheme, the AMC must: (1) send a written communication about the proposed change to each unit holder and issue an advertisement in one English daily with nationwide circulation, as well as in a newspaper in the language of the region where the mutual fund's head office is located; and (2) give unit holders the option to exit at the prevailing Net Asset Value without any exit load.

context: Regulation 5(e): any company or body corporate, having continuous net worth of minimum rupees one hundred crores as per its audited annual accounts for the previous five years prior to filing of the application with the Board for the grant of certificate.
question: A body corporate files an application to promote a credit rating agency in December 2025. Its audited net worth for the preceding years was: 2020-21: Rs 95 crore; 2021-22: Rs 102 crore; 2022-23: Rs 110 crore; 2023-24: Rs 108 crore; 2024-25: Rs 115 crore. Does it meet the Regulation 4(e) promoter eligibility criterion?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, it does not meet the eligibility criterion. Regulation 4(e) requires a continuous net worth of at least Rs 100 crore for each of the five years preceding the application. The body corporate's net worth for 2020-21 was Rs 95 crore, which is below the Rs 100 crore threshold. Since the requirement is for continuous net worth across all five preceding years, failing even one year disqualifies the applicant.

context: Regulation 9(e): the promoter of the credit rating agency, in terms of regulation 4, shall maintain a minimum shareholding of 26% in the credit rating agency for a minimum period of three years from the date of grant of registration by the Board.
question: A CRA's promoter holds 35% of the CRA's shares at the time of registration. The CRA was granted registration on April 1, 2023. Can the promoter legally reduce its shareholding to 20% on June 15, 2026?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, the promoter cannot legally reduce its shareholding to 20% on June 15, 2026. Under Regulation 9(e), the promoter must maintain a minimum shareholding of 26% for at least three years from the date of grant of registration. The CRA was registered on April 1, 2023, and the three-year lock-in period ends on April 1, 2026. While the lock-in has technically expired by June 15, 2026, reducing the shareholding to 20% would fall below the required 26% minimum. The regulation mandates a minimum of 26% during the lock-in period — it does not speak to what happens after, but a drop to 20% during a period where the minimum must be maintained would be a violation if done before the period ends. Since June 15, 2026 is after April 1, 2026, the lock-in has expired — so structurally the restriction no longer applies after that date. However, the regulation only mandates 26% for the minimum three-year period; after that, no floor is specified in this provision. So technically, after April 1, 2026, the promoter may reduce its holding, and June 15, 2026 is past that date. The answer is: yes, it is legally permissible, since the three-year minimum period has already concluded by June 15, 2026.

context: The original definition of 'advertisement' in the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 (clause 2(b)) enumerated specific advertising media: 'every form of advertising, whether in a publication, by display of notices, signs, labels or by means of circulars, catalogues or other documents, by an exhibition of pictures or photographic films, by way of sound broadcasting or television, or in any other manner.' This was substituted by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) (Amendment) Regulations, 2012 (w.e.f. 21-2-2012) with a broader definition: 'all forms of communication issued by or on behalf of the asset management company/mutual fund that may influence investment decisions of any investor/prospective investors.'
question: What key change did the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Amendment Regulations, 2012 make to the definition of 'advertisement'?
YOUR_ANSWER: The original definition of 'advertisement' was a detailed, media-specific list — it enumerated particular forms like publications, television, sound broadcasting, notices, and films. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Amendment Regulations, 2012, effective 21 February 2012, replaced this with a broad, principles-based definition covering all forms of communication issued by or on behalf of the AMC/mutual fund that may influence investment decisions of any investor or prospective investor. The key shift was from a closed enumeration of media to a comprehensive, intent-based definition.

context: Disqualification from being appointed as trustees. 16. (3) No asset management company and no director (including independent director), officer or employee of an asset management company shall be eligible to be appointed as a trustee of any mutual fund.
question: Under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, are directors, officers or employees of an AMC eligible to be appointed as trustees of any mutual fund?
YOUR_ANSWER: No. Under Regulation 16(3) of SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, no asset management company, and no director (including independent director), officer, or employee of an AMC, is eligible to be appointed as a trustee of any mutual fund.

context: Regulation 3(1): No acquirer shall acquire shares or voting rights in a target company which taken together with shares or voting rights held by him and by persons acting in concert entitle them to exercise twenty-five per cent or more of the voting rights in such target company unless the acquirer makes a public announcement of an open offer.
question: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations 2011, what voting rights threshold triggers the mandatory open offer obligation?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under Regulation 3(1), the mandatory open offer obligation is triggered when an acquirer's shareholding or voting rights — together with those of persons acting in concert — reaches or exceeds 25% of the voting rights in the target company.

context: Regulation 5(c) (original): the applicant has a minimum net worth of rupees five crores. [Substituted by SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018, w.e.f. 30-05-2018]: the applicant has a minimum net worth of rupees twenty five crore.
question: When was the minimum net worth requirement for credit rating agency applicants under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 raised, and by how much was it increased?
YOUR_ANSWER: The minimum net worth requirement was raised on 30 May 2018, when the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 came into effect. The requirement was increased from Rs 5 crore to Rs 25 crore — a fivefold increase.

context: Seventh Schedule (historical). Clause 5 (now omitted): The initial issue expenses in respect of any scheme may not exceed six per cent of the funds raised under that scheme. (This clause was omitted by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) (Amendment) Regulations, 2008, w.e.f. 16-4-2008.)
question: What was the maximum initial issue expense ratio for a mutual fund scheme under the original Seventh Schedule, and when was this provision omitted?
YOUR_ANSWER: Under the original Seventh Schedule, the maximum initial issue expenses for a mutual fund scheme were capped at 6% of the funds raised under that scheme. This provision was omitted by the SEBI (Mutual Funds) (Amendment) Regulations, 2008, with effect from 16 April 2008.

context: Regulation 15(1)(d): Category III Alternative Investment Funds shall invest not more than ten per cent of the investable funds in an Investee Company, directly or through investment in units of other Alternative Investment Funds and the large value funds for accredited investors of Category III Alternative Investment Funds may invest up to twenty per cent of the investable funds in an Investee Company, directly or through investment in units of other Alternative Investment Funds.
question: What is the single-investee concentration limit for Category III Alternative Investment Funds under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: For regular Category III AIFs, the single-investee concentration limit is 10% of the investable funds (whether investing directly or through units of other AIFs). However, for large value funds for accredited investors within Category III, this limit is relaxed to 20% of the investable funds.

context:

Revised Press Release (March 21, 2026) — Uttarakhand: 1000 (09 year), 1000 (20 year), 1500 (18 year). Total Uttarakhand (revised): 3500 crore.

Original Press Release (March 20, 2026) — Uttarakhand: 1000 (09 year), 1000 (20 year), 1280 (18 year). Total Uttarakhand (original): 3280 crore.
question: Do the original and revised press releases state the same borrowing amount for Uttarakhand's 18-year tenor securities in the March 24, 2026 auction?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they do not state the same amount. The original press release of March 20, 2026 stated that Uttarakhand's 18-year tenor offering was Rs 1,280 crore, while the revised press release of March 21, 2026 increased this to Rs 1,500 crore. The two documents differ on this figure.

context: Where a certificate has been granted to an intermediary on a permanent basis, the certificate may continue to be valid under these regulations subject to the condition that the intermediary shall, within two years of commencement of these regulations in relation to such intermediary, furnish the information in Form A to the Board and upload the information in Part I thereof on the website specified by the Board: Provided that the time specified in clause (b) may be extended by the Board up to a period of six months on sufficient reasons being shown by the intermediary.
question: Under SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations 2008, an intermediary holding a permanent certificate at the time of commencement of these regulations must furnish Form A information within two years. What is the maximum total time available if SEBI grants an extension?
YOUR_ANSWER: The base period is two years from commencement of the regulations. SEBI may extend this by up to six months on sufficient cause. So the maximum total time available to furnish Form A information is two years and six months from the date of commencement of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008 in relation to that intermediary.

context: Regulation 21(1): Every credit rating agency shall keep and maintain, for a minimum period of five years, the following books of accounts, records and documents: (a) copy of its balance sheet; (b) a copy of its profit and loss account; (c) a copy of the auditor's report; (d) a copy of the agreement entered into with each client; (e) information supplied by each client; (f) correspondence with each client; (g) ratings assigned, including upgradation and downgradation; (h) rating notes considered by the rating committee; (i) record of decisions of the rating committee; (j) letter assigning rating; (k) particulars of fees charged.
question: For how long and what types of records must a credit rating agency maintain under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
YOUR_ANSWER: A credit rating agency must maintain records for a minimum period of five years. The records to be maintained include: balance sheets, profit and loss accounts, auditor's reports, agreements with each client, information supplied by clients, correspondence with clients, ratings assigned (including upgrades and downgrades), rating notes considered by the rating committee, records of rating committee decisions, letters assigning ratings, and particulars of fees charged.

context: Each intermediary shall prominently display a photocopy of the certificate at all its offices including branch offices. The intermediary shall also prominently display the name and contact details of the compliance officer to whom complaint may be made in the event of any investor grievance.
question: What two things must a SEBI-registered intermediary prominently display at all its offices, including branch offices?
YOUR_ANSWER: Every SEBI-registered intermediary must prominently display at all its offices, including branch offices: (1) a photocopy of its SEBI registration certificate; and (2) the name and contact details of the compliance officer, so investors know who to approach in case of a grievance.

context: An issuer shall be eligible to make an initial public offer only if: (a) it has net tangible assets of at least three crore rupees, calculated on a restated and consolidated basis, in each of the preceding three full years (of twelve months each), of which not more than fifty per cent. are held in monetary assets; (b) it has an average operating profit of at least fifteen crore rupees, calculated on a restated and consolidated basis, during the preceding three years (of twelve months each), with operating profit in each of these preceding three years; (c) it has a net worth of at least one crore rupees in each of the preceding three full years (of twelve months each), calculated on a restated and consolidated basis.
question: What is the minimum average operating profit an issuer must have over the preceding three years to be eligible to make an initial public offer under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018?
YOUR_ANSWER: The issuer must have an average operating profit of at least Rs 15 crore, calculated on a restated and consolidated basis, during the preceding three years of twelve months each. Additionally, the issuer must have had operating profit in each of those three individual years — not just on average.

context: Regulation 14(1): Units of close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be listed on stock exchange subject to a minimum tradable lot of one crore rupees. (2) Listing of Alternative Investment Fund units shall be permitted only after final close of the fund or scheme.
question: What are the conditions under which the units of a close-ended AIF may be listed on a stock exchange under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: Units of a close-ended AIF may be listed on a stock exchange subject to two conditions: (1) the minimum tradable lot must be Rs 1 crore; and (2) listing is permitted only after the final close of the fund or scheme.

context: Section A of the Directions on implementation of Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) shall come into force with immediate effect. Section B of the Directions on implementation of Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) shall come into effect from January 01, 2027.
question: Under the RBI Master Direction on Unique Identifiers in Financial Markets 2026, when does the section on Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) implementation come into effect?
YOUR_ANSWER: The section on Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) implementation under Section B of the RBI Master Direction on Unique Identifiers in Financial Markets 2026 comes into effect from January 01, 2027.

context:
Passage A:
The Manager or Sponsor shall have a continuing interest in the Alternative Investment Fund of not less than two and half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower, in the form of investment in the Alternative Investment Fund and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees.

Passage B:
Provided that for Category III Alternative Investment Fund, the continuing interest shall be not less than five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower.
question: Do the two passages prescribe different minimum continuing interest thresholds for Category I/II AIFs versus Category III AIFs under SEBI AIF Regulations 2012?
YOUR_ANSWER: Yes, the two passages prescribe different thresholds. Passage A sets the general rule: the minimum continuing interest for the Manager or Sponsor is 2.5% of the corpus or Rs 5 crore, whichever is lower. Passage B introduces a higher threshold specifically for Category III AIFs: the continuing interest must be not less than 5% of the corpus or Rs 10 crore, whichever is lower. So Category III AIFs face a stricter requirement compared to Category I and II AIFs.

context:
Passage A:
Regulation 2(1)(pa) (before November 2025 amendment): 'large value fund for accredited investors' means an Alternative Investment Fund or scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund in which each investor (other than the Manager, Sponsor, employees or directors of the Alternative Investment Fund or employees or directors of the Manager) is an accredited investor and invests not less than seventy crore rupees.

Passage B:
Regulation 2(1)(pa) (as amended w.e.f. 19-11-2025): 'large value fund for accredited investors' means an Alternative Investment Fund or scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund in which each investor (other than the Manager, Sponsor, employees or directors of the Alternative Investment Fund or employees or directors of the Manager) is an accredited investor and invests not less than twenty-five crore rupees.
question: Does the original definition of 'large value fund for accredited investors' and the November 2025-amended definition impose the same minimum investment threshold per investor?
YOUR_ANSWER: No, they do not impose the same threshold. The original definition required each investor (excluding certain exempted persons) to invest not less than Rs 70 crore. The amended definition, effective 19 November 2025, reduced this minimum investment threshold to Rs 25 crore per investor. So the two definitions differ significantly — the November 2025 amendment lowered the bar for what qualifies as a large value fund for accredited investors.
